"A person." The general rule is that there are 3 categories of Canaanite slave. The first is a slave who underwent brit milah and accepted the mitzvot, like a full convert, except that a convert is obligated in all mitzvot incumbent upon a man, while a slave is obligated in the mitzvot incumbent upon a woman. The second is an eved toshav, analogous to a ger toshav. The third is an ordinary gentile slave, like any other gentile. The latter 2 are without brit milah. Their laws are explained below.

"Regarding the rest," etc. Yevamos 48b derives from "so that your servant may rest" the case of a slave who underwent brit milah.

"Who underwent brit milah and immersion." We rule like R' Yose there and like R' Yochanan that one is not a convert until both brit milah and immersion have been performed. The same applies to a slave, because their law in this respect is the same. See there concerning the case of Binyamin.

"And accepted upon himself." This follows Rif, who requires formal acceptance, based on the statement in Yevamos 48b, "if he did not wish," etc. See Rosh at the end of siman 38, Rif there, and the end of chapter 19 of Shabbos.

"The mitzvot that apply to a slave." See Chagigah, chapter 1, concerning all the mitzvot in which a slave is obligated.

"But if," etc. Kerisus 9a, where R' Shimon distinguishes a ger toshav; the halacha there follows R' Shimon.

"Rather, he accepted," etc. Avodah Zarah 64b, in accordance with the Sages. See Rashba, responsum 59, at length.

"The same applies, and it is permitted." Kerisus there.

"But not," etc. Kerisus there and Yevamos there, from the verse "and the son of your maidservant shall be refreshed," as explained below.

"And it is forbidden to every Jew." This is inferred from the qualification that he may work "for himself." Moreover, the law is analogous to a ger toshav, who has no master. The exclusion therefore must mean that only work for himself is permitted, but a Jew may not command him to work.

"To tell him." The prohibition here concerns specifically instructing him, and this is the distinction between another Jew and his master, as explained below.

"And if he did not accept." Maggid Mishneh writes in the name of Rashba, based on the passage in Yevamos concerning "the son of your maidservant" and an without brit milah slave. Rashba explains the verse in this manner because the baraita does not use the expression eved toshav as it does in Kerisus, and because otherwise no separate verse would be necessary, since he would already be included in the law of a ger toshav.

"According to this." Regarding the prohibition of melacha, there is no practical distinction from another non-Jew with respect to instructing him, because telling any non-Jew to perform melacha is forbidden, as stated in Shabbos 150a. Likewise, work for his master is forbidden, as explained below. The difference is that with an ordinary non-Jew the prohibition is rabbinic, whereas here it is Torah-level, as appears in Yevamos. The practical consequence is as stated immediately afterward.

"For the needs," etc. See Shabbos 129a.

"Likewise." Beitzah 6a; see also 22a.

"And some disagree," etc. Meaning, they disagree regarding a full gentile slave whom the earlier view equates with an eved toshav, implying that even another Jew may not instruct him. The dissenting authorities permit another Jew to instruct him because the Torah warned only the master concerning the slave's rest, as stated in Yevamos. The passage in Kerisus that compares the slave to a ger toshav applies specifically to an eved toshav. Accordingly, another Jew who is not his master may instruct him to perform what is needed for an ill person. The phrase "and some disagree" therefore refers back to the statement concerning even an ordinary gentile slave. Eshel Avraham writes likewise, although Beit Yosef did not cite a dissenting opinion on this point.

"Nevertheless," etc., "and another Jew," etc., "provided," etc. All these distinctions are explained in Shabbos 151a: if the slave acts on his own initiative, one need not stop him when the work is not being done for the master's benefit. This is no more stringent than the law of a minor, whose father is likewise commanded concerning his rest, yet when the minor acts independently for himself the father need not stop him in every case.

For the master, however, anything the slave does is ordinarily presumed to be for the master's benefit. Regarding another Jew, even if the slave knows that the Jew will benefit, so long as the Jew did not instruct him and the slave began on his own initiative, the act is presumed to be for the slave's own benefit or profit, and the Jew need not stop him unless it is clear that he acts for the Jew.

"Provided that he does not benefit." Rabbinically, the slave is no better than any other non-Jew who knowingly performs melacha for a Jew. The Jew may not benefit from that melacha on Shabbos, as stated at the beginning of siman 276.

The 6 distinctions stated here are reflected in the Mishnah: a non-Jew who kindled a lamp for himself may be used; if he kindled it for a Jew it may not. One need not tell a non-Jew who comes to extinguish a fire not to do so when he acts on his own initiative. A slave acting for his master is different because his actions are presumed to be for the master's benefit. These principles explain the rulings here and the distinctions between work for himself, for his master, and for another Jew.

Which slave one is commanded to rest on Shabbos. It contains 3 seifim: A person is commanded concerning the Shabbos rest of his slave who underwent brit milah and immersion for the sake of slavery and accepted upon himself the mitzvot that apply to a slave. If, however, he did not undergo brit milah and immersion but accepted upon himself the 7 Noahide mitzvot, he is like a ger toshav. He may perform melacha on Shabbos for himself, but not for his master, and every Jew is forbidden to instruct him to perform melacha on Shabbos for the needs of a Jew, even one who is not his master. If he did not accept upon himself even the 7 Noahide mitzvot, some authorities hold that the same restrictions apply to him, while others permit another Jew who is not his master to instruct him in circumstances in which instruction of such a slave is permitted. {Rama: In any event, the master must not permit his slave to perform melacha for the master's benefit, and if the slave acts on his own initiative the distinctions stated by the authorities regarding benefit and protest apply.}

Seif katan 1, "concerning his slave," etc. Two verses are written. One says, "so that your servant and maidservant may rest like you." This refers to a slave who underwent brit milah and immersion for the sake of slavery and accepted all the mitzvot incumbent upon slaves, meaning all mitzvot in which a woman is obligated. Shabbos is included among these mitzvot. Therefore such a slave may not perform melacha on Shabbos even for himself.

The second verse says, "and the son of your maidservant and the stranger shall be refreshed." The Sages expounded this as referring to a gentile slave who is bodily owned by a Jew but did not undergo brit milah or immersion, and accepted only the 7 Noahide mitzvot. Every Jew is forbidden to instruct such a slave to perform melacha on Shabbos. For his own needs, however, the slave may perform melacha, because Shabbos is not included among the 7 Noahide mitzvot.

A slave who is bodily owned by a Jew but did not undergo brit milah or immersion and did not accept any mitzvah, not even the 7 Noahide mitzvot, is the subject of a dispute among the authorities whether we are likewise commanded concerning his Shabbos rest, as will be explained.

"And likewise, if someone died on the first day of Yom Tov," etc., "it is forbidden to tell a Jewish-owned slave." See siman 526 in Beit Yosef. Ramban there inclines to permit use of a slave who did not undergo brit milah and immersion. The approach of the Shulchan Aruch here follows Baal Halachot Gedolot. Tosefet Shabbos sought to read this distinction into the concluding words, "and some disagree"; see there.

"And some disagree and permit this." As explained in Mishnah Berurah, where the slave did not accept the 7 Noahide mitzvot, the Torah prohibition concerning his Shabbos rest applies according to this view only to his master and not to another Jew. This appears to apply specifically where the slave is not acting for his master's benefit. If the slave is doing the melacha to please or benefit the master, the master must stop him. Where it is clear that the act is genuinely for the slave himself, there is no obligation to prevent it.

For another Jew, the law is more lenient. Even when the slave knows that another Jew will benefit, if that Jew did not command him and the slave initiated the work himself, it may be presumed that he acts for his own benefit, such as for payment or another advantage. The prohibition arises when the Jew instructs him, or where it is evident that he is acting specifically for the Jew.

"Permitted." See the end of siman 252, seif 2, where in certain rabbinic cases one must nevertheless protest against a non-Jew's work.

"Provided that he does not benefit." This restriction is rabbinic. The slave is not more lenient than another non-Jew who performs melacha for a Jew, from whose Shabbos melacha the Jew may not benefit, as stated at the beginning of siman 276.

"Some say every slave," etc. This view holds that the Torah did not warn a Jew concerning the Shabbos rest of a gentile slave unless the slave accepted at least some mitzvot, namely the 7 Noahide mitzvot, as Beit Yosef explains. Avnei Nezer cites several authorities who act stringently in accordance with the first view. It is likewise forbidden to instruct an apostate Jew or a Karaite to perform melacha on Shabbos or Yom Tov because of lifnei iver. [Pri Megadim]

"Every slave," etc. Regarding a slave who also did not undergo brit milah or immersion, see Tosafos and Pri Megadim.

"It is forbidden for him to go out," etc. The remaining discussion concerns the slave's seal and the laws of carrying it on Shabbos. Where there are 2 grounds for leniency, such as a clay seal hanging from his neck, it may be permitted. A clay seal has little independent value, so if it breaks there is no substantial concern that he will carry it. Where there is only 1 ground for leniency, such as when the seal hangs from the garment, or when it is metal and therefore valuable, carrying in a public domain is forbidden under the distinctions explained below.

"Not on his garment." If the seal breaks, the slave may fear that his master will say he removed it in order to appear free. He may therefore fold his garment to conceal the place of the seal and carry the garment on his shoulder as a burden.

"And if it is metal," etc. Because it is valuable, the master is particular that it not be lost. There is therefore concern that if it breaks the slave will carry it 4 amot in a public domain.

"In every manner." Even if it hangs from his neck, when the slave made the seal for himself he does not fear his master if he removes it. There is therefore concern that he may take it in his hand and carry it in the public domain.

These distinctions show that the laws here involve 2 separate questions: the master's command concerning the slave's Shabbos rest, and the ordinary Shabbos prohibitions that apply to the slave's own carrying. Each is governed by its own rationale and set of distinctions.

"Did not undergo brit milah." Regarding a slave who follows Jewish practice but has not yet undergone brit milah and immersed before a beit din, whether he may be buried on the second day of Yom Tov and whether he must be exhumed if he was already buried in a Jewish cemetery, see Responsa D.A., siman 19.

"Complete." See Responsa Beit Yehudah, siman 13.
